content:
Using the corrected chesslike condition: in a chesslike \(2\times2\), the two cells on each diagonal have the same color, and the two diagonals have opposite colors.

Consider the \(5\times5\) array of all \(2\times2\) subsquares. Mark a subsquare if it is chesslike.  
If three marked subsquares are consecutive along a NW-SE diagonal, say at positions
\[
(i,j),\ (i+1,j+1),\ (i+2,j+2),
\]
then the four board cells
\[
(i,j),\ (i+1,j+1),\ (i+2,j+2),\ (i+3,j+3)
\]
are all the same color, because each chesslike \(2\times2\) has equal NW-SE diagonal cells. This violates the condition.  
So in each NW-SE diagonal of the \(5\times5\) array, there cannot be three consecutive marked squares.

The NW-SE diagonal lengths in a \(5\times5\) array are
\[
1,2,3,4,5,4,3,2,1.
\]
With no three consecutive marks, the maximum marks on a diagonal of length \(L\) are:
\[
L=1,2,3,4,5 \implies 1,2,2,3,4.
\]
Thus the total number of chesslike squares is at most
\[
1+2+2+3+4+3+2+2+1=20.
\]

This bound is attainable. For example, color the rows as
\[
\begin{array}{cccccc}
R&G&R&G&R&G\\
G&R&G&R&G&R\\
R&G&R&G&R&G\\
R&G&R&G&R&G\\
G&R&G&R&G&R\\
R&G&R&G&R&G
\end{array}
\]
Rows \(1\)–\(2\), \(2\)–\(3\), \(4\)–\(5\), and \(5\)–\(6\) each produce all \(5\) chesslike squares in those gaps, while rows \(3\)–\(4\) produce none. So there are \(20\) chesslike squares.

Therefore the maximal possible number is
\[
\boxed{20}.
\]
